editorial_contributions.text: Summary: A globally adaptive algorithm for numerical cubature of a vector of functions over a collection of \(n\)-dimensional simplices is described. The algorithm is based on a subdivision strategy that chooses for subdivision at each stage the subregion (of the input simplices) with the largest estimated error. This subregion is divided into two, three or four equal volume subregions by cutting selected edges. These edges are selected using information about the smoothness of the integrands in the edge directions. The algorithm allows a choice from several embedded cubature rule sequences for approximate integration and error estimation. A Fortran 95 implementation as a part of CUBPACK is also discussed. Testing of the algorithm is described.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Density estimation is a building block for many other statistical methods, such as classification, nonparametric testing, and data compression. In this paper, we focus on a non-parametric approach to multivariate density estimation, and study its asymptotic properties under both frequentist and Bayesian settings. The estimated density function is obtained by considering a sequence of approximating spaces to the space of densities. These spaces consist of piecewise constant density functions supported by binary partitions with increasing complexity. To obtain an estimate, the partition is learned by maximizing either the likelihood of the corresponding histogram on that partition, or the marginal posterior probability of the partition under a suitable prior. We analyze the convergence rate of the maximum likelihood estimator and the posterior concentration rate of the Bayesian estimator, and conclude that for a relatively rich class of density functions the rate does not directly depend on the dimension. We also show that the Bayesian method can adapt to the unknown smoothness of the density function. The method is applied to several specific function classes and explicit rates are obtained. These include spatially sparse functions, functions of bounded variation, and Hölder continuous functions. We also introduce an ensemble approach, obtained by aggregating multiple density estimates fit under carefully designed perturbations, and show that for density functions lying in a Hölder space (\( \mathcal{H}^{1, \beta}\), \(0 < \beta \leq 1\)), the ensemble method can achieve minimax convergence rate up to a logarithmic term, while the corresponding rate of the density estimator based on a single partition is suboptimal for this function class.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: This paper studies the task of learning transformation models for ranking problems, ordinal regression and survival analysis. The present contribution describes a machine learning approach termed MINLIP. The key insight is to relate ranking criteria as the Area Under the Curve to monotone transformation functions. Consequently, the notion of a Lipschitz smoothness constant is found to be useful for complexity control for learning transformation models, much in a similar vein as the 'margin' is for Support Vector Machines for classification. The use of this model structure in the context of high dimensional data, as well as for estimating non-linear, and additive models based on primal-dual kernel machines, and for sparse models is indicated. Given \(n\) observations, the present method solves a quadratic program existing of \(O(n)\) constraints and \(O(n)\) unknowns, where most existing risk minimization approaches to ranking problems typically result in algorithms with \(O(n^{2})\) constraints or unknowns. We specify the MINLIP method for three different cases: the first one concerns the preference learning problem. Secondly it is specified how to adapt the method to ordinal regression with a finite set of ordered outcomes. Finally, it is shown how the method can be used in the context of survival analysis where one models failure times, typically subject to censoring. The current approach is found to be particularly useful in this context as it can handle, in contrast with the standard statistical model for analyzing survival data, all types of censoring in a straightforward way, and because of the explicit relation with the Proportional Hazard and Accelerated Failure Time models. The advantage of the current method is illustrated on different benchmark data sets, as well as for estimating a model for cancer survival based on different micro-array and clinical data sets.

editorial_contributions.text:
This article is situated in computational algebraic number theory, more specifically in the design and analysis of subexponential algorithms for computing ideal class groups of large-degree number fields, with a clear eye toward cryptographic parameter selection and cryptanalytic practice. Its main contribution is the proposal and empirical evaluation of a pseudo-random walk on ideals that replaces the random ideal generation strategy in Gélin's relation collection algorithm, leading to a substantial practical speed-up while preserving the same heuristic asymptotic complexity.


 The work is anchored in the standard subexponential framework for class group computation, where running times are expressed in terms of the classical
\[
L_N(\alpha,c) \;=\; \exp\!\Big((c+o(1))(\log N)^\alpha (\log\log N)^{1-\alpha}\Big),
\]
and builds directly on Hafner-McCurley-type algorithms and their generalizations by Buchmann, Biasse-Fieker and, most prominently, Gélin's simplified large-degree algorithm based on ideal reduction and BKZ. Within this well-established index-calculus paradigm, relation collection proceeds by generating principal ideals with bounded norm and testing them for smoothness over a factor base of prime ideals bounded by a parameter \(B\). The article preserves Gélin's analytic parameter regime -- most notably the block size \(\beta\) for BKZ and the smoothness bound \(B\) chosen as \(L_{|\Delta_K|}(2\alpha/3,c_b)\) -- and intervenes only in the ``concrete'' cost of producing each candidate ideal, which is precisely where it introduces the pseudo-random walk.

Technically, the authors replace the repeated exponentiation and multiplication of random primes from the factor base by a structured walk on a precomputed table \(T\) of products of primes below Bach's bound. Each entry of \(T\) is a product of \(\kappa\) or \(\kappa+1\) primes \(q_i\) with \(\mathrm{N}(q_i)\leq C\), where \(C = 12(\log|\Delta_K|)^2\) is Bach's bound; the table is constructed in a preprocessing phase by random partitioning of this ``small-prime'' set and has each prime represented \(R\) times. A hash function \(H\) from ideals to indices in \(T\) then defines a walk
\[
a_{i+1} \;=\; a_i \cdot T[H(a_i)]\!,
\]
starting from an initial ideal that itself is a product of a small number \(\kappa_0\) of primes below \(C\). At each step, the algorithm performs BKZ-reduction on the lattice associated with \(a_i\), extracts a short vector corresponding to an element \(x_v\), and tests the ideal \(b\) defined by \((x_v)=a_i b\) for \(B\)-smoothness. Under the heuristic assumption that the visited ideals are ``random enough'' in the sense that their smoothness behaviour matches that of genuinely random ideals of comparable norm, the authors argue that the smoothness probabilities and thus the asymptotic complexity remain as in Gélin's analysis.

In the broader landscape of current research, the article positions itself as a complementary, implementation-focused contribution alongside complexity-driven advances such as Biasse's \(L(1/3)\) algorithms for special classes of fields, Gélin-Joux's work on small defining polynomials, and sieving-based relation collection for particular number field families. Rather than seeking a better asymptotic exponent, the present work refines the ``inner loop'' of class group algorithms in the large-degree regime \(\alpha \in (3/4,1]\), where the existing theory already yields subexponential complexity but concrete performance is highly sensitive to the cost of ideal arithmetic and lattice reductions. The empirical methodology -- Magma implementations of both Gélin's original method and the new walk-based variant, tested on number fields of degrees \(10,15,20,25\) with discriminants up to roughly \(256\) bits -- makes the article resonate with recent efforts that bridge the gap between analytic number theory and cryptographic practice, for example in the analysis of CSIDH-like schemes and more general class-group-based cryptosystems.

The practical applicability of the results is twofold. On the one hand, any implementation of class group (and regulator) computation that uses ideal-reduction-based relation collection for general number fields can incorporate the proposed pseudo-random walk layer almost as a drop-in replacement for the random exponentiation step, at the cost of a one-time precomputation of the table \(T\). The reported timing results suggest a factor of about three improvement in relation collection time for the tested fields, even after accounting for the slightly lower empirical smoothness probabilities along the walk, and the authors verify that the basic requirements for relation collection -- namely that the number of relations exceeds the factor base size and that each prime ideal below Bach's bound appears in at least one relation -- are still met. On the other hand, improved class group algorithms have indirect impact on the assessment of security margins for cryptographic primitives defined over class groups of imaginary quadratic or higher-degree number fields, including CSIDH-type key exchange, unknown-order groups for accumulators and SNARKs, and constructions relying on class groups as hidden-order groups. While the experiments are carried out for relatively modest discriminant sizes from a cryptanalytic perspective, the algorithmic pattern is generic and may serve as a building block in larger-scale implementations or in hybrid methods that combine algebraic techniques with sieving or quantum subroutines.

At the same time, the paper's focus on heuristic arguments and moderate-size experiments leaves several avenues that would be valuable to explore in subsequent research. The pseudo-random walk is analysed only at the level of its effect on norms and smoothness probabilities, with randomness modelled by the assumption that the hash function output is uniformly distributed and that successive ideals behave like independent random samples; a more refined study of the walk as a Markov chain on the ideal class group, including mixing properties, structural biases, or dependence on the choice of \(H\) and the construction of \(T\), could help to explain the observed slight degradation in smoothness probability and perhaps suggest improved designs. From a computational perspective, the current implementation uses BKZ with small block size (effectively close to LLL in practice) and fixed precision; an in-depth exploration of the interaction between walk length \(\lambda\), precision growth, and norm control -- possibly including adaptive precision strategies or alternative reduction techniques -- could further optimise the trade-off between the cost of each step and the quality of the resulting short vectors. Finally, the experiments are limited to a small number of medium-size fields; a systematic campaign on larger discriminants and varying degrees, including fields tailored to cryptographic constructions such as those underlying CSIDH, would clarify the scalability of the approach and its quantitative impact on concrete security estimates. In conjunction with these directions, it would also be natural to investigate hybrid strategies that combine the proposed walk with sieving-based relation collection or with quantum subroutines in the setting of post-quantum class group algorithms, thereby situating this practical speed-up within a more comprehensive algorithmic toolkit for class group computation.

editorial_contributions.text:
The Zakharov system, which describes the propagation of Langmuir waves in a plasma, is considered. The authors employ a well-established method, i.e., a Lie-Trotter splitting in time combined with a Fourier collocation in space, which has been proven to work well through extensive numerical testing. However, a rigorous error analysis of such methods has been lacking in the literature. The complexity lies in the formal loss of spatial regularity (loss of spatial derivatives) in the Zakharov system, which the numerical method and analysis need to be able to overcome.

Hence, this article is devoted to a rigorous error analysis of the method considered here. The authors prove first-order convergence in time and high-order convergence in space, depending on the regularity of the exact solution. A CFL-type step-size restriction on the discretization parameter is developed, indicating the circumstance under which the error bounds holds. Given the temporal and spatial error bounds obtained, this CFL condition is in fact a natural restriction on the discretization parameters. Numerical experiments are utilised to show that this condition is not only sufficient but also necessary for convergence.
